title: Float-test eggs: lower each into a bowl of water without cracking it, then lift the floating one out into a dish
instruction: Lower each egg into the bowl of water without cracking it, then lift any egg that floats out into the small dish and leave the others in the bowl.
context: The float test is the kitchen check many people learn for eggs of unknown age: in a bowl of cold water a fresh egg sinks and lies on its side, an older one sinks and stands on end, and a very old one floats and is set aside (USU Extension; Egg Safety Center). The hard part is the handling. An egg can crack if it is squeezed hard or let fall onto glass from about a centimeter, so each egg must be picked up with a light grip and let go only at the water's surface. The floater then has to be picked out of the water: a wet, smooth egg standing upright, with only a few millimeters showing, held lightly enough not to crack it and firmly enough not to slip, and set down in the dish. In the sim the eggs look alike, so the robot finds out which one floats only once it is in the water; the score needs all three tested in the water first.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, on the table top (x forward, y left). Bowl: clear glass 2.5 qt mixing bowl (Anchor Hocking 81575L20: top 8 5/8 in, bottom 4 5/8 in, 4 1/4 in high), centered at x 32, y 0, holding 1.2 L of cold tap water (7.5 cm deep), on a thin non-slip silicone mat. Eggs: three brown eggs lying on their sides on a red cotton tea towel folded to 13 x 22 cm (centered at x 30, y 23), long axes along x, their middles at y 16, 23 and 30. Two sink and one floats (blunt end up, about 5 mm showing); which place holds the floater is shuffled per trial. Sim: US Large eggs, 56.7 mm long x 42.1 mm across: a fresh egg (57.0 g, lies on its side), an older egg (53.9 g, stands on end) and a floater (51.1 g). Real trial: two fresh US Large brown eggs from a new carton (both sink and lie on their side) and one brown hollow plastic egg (BestPysanky dummy nest egg, 57 x 40 mm) weighted with steel BBs, locked in with modelling clay, so that it floats blunt end up with 4-7 mm showing (about 46.4 g); the operator knows the floater by feel. Discard dish: clear glass 8.5 oz ramekin (Duralex Ovenchef: top 3 7/8 in, 2 in high), empty, at x 30, y -20.5, on the mat. Nothing else on the table; arms in the ready pose.
scoring: 0 if at any time an egg that is not held (both fingertips of one hand pressing it from opposite sides) moves faster than 0.40 m/s in any direction, or an egg, held or not, first touches the glass, table, towel or another egg faster than that, or while touching one has its velocity change by more than that in one physics step: the speed of a free fall of 8 mm (real trial: video shows it let go more than 8 mm above the water, the glass or the table, thrown, or knocked or rammed into something); or an egg is pressed harder than 38 N in 3 of any 4 physics steps (1/80 s) or 76 N in one (1/240 s), by any one robot link, either arm's links together, both arms' links together, or everything else together (glass, table, towel, the other eggs) (real trial: these limits are scored in the sim only; a real egg with a visibly cracked shell scores 0; the plastic floater cannot crack, so a hard squeeze on it is not caught); or an egg leaves the table; or (real trial) the bowl is knocked off its mat or water spills over its rim. Otherwise 0 until every egg has been tested: each has sat in the bowl's water, not touched by the robot, for 1 s. 0.25 once all three have been tested; 0.5 and the floater out of the bowl, with the other two lying or standing on the bowl's floor (lowest point within 1.2 cm of it) and not touched; 0.75 and the floater on the ramekin's floor (lowest point within 1.2 cm of it, its middle inside the ramekin) and not touched; 1.0 and every egg at rest (under 1 cm/s) with every link of both arms 2 cm or more from every egg, held 1 s. A good egg taken out of the bowl, or the floater left in it, stays at 0.25. Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Lift the three eggs out, dry them and lay them back on the towel at their marks; top the bowl up to 1.2 L of cold water. Sinkers: two fresh eggs from a new carton, kept in the refrigerator between sessions; a cracked one is replaced from the carton. Floater, once (about 15 minutes): stand the brown plastic egg hole up (blunt end) in an egg carton; drop in 4.5 mm steel BBs (Daisy .177) a few at a time, floating it in cold tap water after each few, until it floats blunt end up (hole above the water) with about 10 mm showing; narrow end down, push modelling clay in with a skewer onto the BBs so they cannot shift, then add small bits of clay, floating it after each, until it floats with 5-7 mm showing; fill the hole with clay, tape over it and check once more: 4-7 mm showing (about 46.4 g). Before each session (1 minute): put the three in cold tap water; both real eggs sink and the floater floats blunt end up with 4-7 mm showing. A floater that sits lower has let in water: replace it. Robot: cover each finger from pad to gripper body with a nitrile glove finger or thin silicone sleeve, taped below the body clear of the finger's slide, dried between trials; the operator stops the trial if water reaches the gripper body.
fidelity: No fluid is simulated: a force model adds buoyancy (from the sloped bowl's water level) and quadratic drag (Cd 0.5); no waves, slosh or surface tension; fingers don't push water. Each egg is a rigid egg-curve hull, its mass and center of mass set by its air cell. Cracks are judged from speed and force. Real trial: both sinkers are fresh (the sim's older sinker stands); the plastic floater is 5% narrower and rights itself more stiffly.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0; demo: 1.0 in 3 of 3 runs (scripted, fixed plan, EGG_SEED=0)
